Complex Systems Analysis and Modelling

发表于2026-08-11|更新于2026-09-07|NUS semester 1
|总字数:31.2k

Complex systems connect microscopic interactions to macroscopic patterns. Probability distributions describe fluctuations and extreme events, network models explain how connections form, and graph metrics quantify the resulting structure. The key tools are the central limit theorem, stable distributions, power laws, preferential attachment, and network algorithms.

A formula is only useful with its conditions: identify the random variable, graph type, and normalization convention before substituting numbers.

On smaller screens, wide equations and tables can be scrolled horizontally.

Introduction: Why Study Complex Systems?

From Individuals to the Whole: Where Complexity Arises

The defining feature of a complex system is more than a large number of parts: interactions among many individuals produce structures and behaviors that an isolated individual does not possess. Four useful characteristics are many-body, autonomous, interaction, and emergence. These refer to many constituent units, decentralized autonomous activity, interactions that often involve nonlinear effects, and the resulting patterns or collective behavior. They provide a framework for recognizing complex systems rather than mathematical axioms that every such system must satisfy exactly.

Autonomy means that overall order need not be designed step by step by a central controller. Emergence means that new observable regularities appear at the collective level; knowing the properties of an individual constituent is not enough to read off the behavior of the whole.

Example Local mechanism or individual level Collective phenomenon illustrated
Army ants and ant rafts Individuals coordinate through local information, including contact with nearby individuals Self-organization, resource efficiency, and collective capabilities
Bird flocks Individuals adjust their motion and influence one another Large-scale synchronization and collective behavior
Fireflies and applause Individual oscillations or rhythms are influenced by others Spontaneous synchronization and pattern formation
Stadium waves Responses to nearby participants and the number of people participating A critical number of participants and a collective response resembling a phase transition
Traffic, cities, and epidemics Networks of people, roads, contacts, and feedback Congestion, spatial organization, and spreading

The Uses and Limits of Reductionism

Reductionism seeks to understand the whole through its components and their interactions. It provides a starting point for microscopic models. Complex systems, however, involve correlations, feedback, and behavior across scales, so simply adding the results for isolated individuals linearly does not explain the whole.

For example, knowing how a single bird flies does not directly predict how a flock turns; we must also specify how each bird responds to other birds. Physical approaches seek common regularities across systems whose details differ, a property known as universality. This usually requires translating the question into measurable macroscopic quantities, such as distribution tails, the degree of synchronization, network connectivity, or clustering.

How to structure a short answer: Identify the individuals, explain their interactions, identify the collective phenomenon, and explain why the properties of an isolated individual are insufficient to determine that phenomenon. Saying only that “the system is large and complicated” is not enough.

Modelling Tools and Their Connections

  • Agent-based models: Specify individual states and rules for actions or interactions, then observe the aggregate behavior. A cellular automaton usually places states on discrete lattice sites and updates them according to neighborhood rules.

  • Complex networks: Represent individuals as nodes and interactions as edges. Distributions describe what the data look like, while networks express who interacts with whom. The same local rules can produce different macroscopic outcomes on different connection structures.

  • Nonlinear dynamics and chaos: Nonlinearity allows a response to be disproportionate to its input. Chaos concerns motion in deterministic systems that is highly sensitive to initial conditions. Complex systems may be ordered or chaotic; “complex” does not mean “random” or “chaotic.”

  • Disorder, heterogeneity, and pattern formation: Real systems differ in their connections, individual properties, or coupling strengths. The question is how these differences affect the emergence of order.

  • Phase transitions and criticality: Changing a control parameter can qualitatively change a system’s macroscopic behavior. Statistical physics provides tools for studying macroscopic phases through microscopic interactions; complex-systems research extends such methods to irregular, heterogeneous structures.

  • Self-organized criticality (SOC): Some driven systems may approach a critical state through their own dynamics. A sandpile provides an intuitive example. Observing a power law does not by itself prove that a system exhibits SOC.

  • Power laws, heavy tails, and scale-free behavior: Large events can be more common than a normal model predicts, suggesting that the assumptions behind a normal approximation may fail. A power law is a testable statistical regularity; it does not automatically identify a unique microscopic mechanism.

A Unifying Line of Reasoning

If many contributions can reasonably be treated as an additive combination of independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance, the CLT supplies a normal baseline prediction. When data depart substantially from that prediction, examine independence, the finiteness of the variance, whether the variable is actually a sum, and whether sampling mixes different mechanisms. Stable distributions and power laws offer another possible class of statistical structures, while growth and preferential attachment provide a specific mechanism that can generate a power law in a network. Network metrics then turn a complicated connection pattern into quantities that can be calculated and compared.

Concept check: If a group of people synchronizes while watching the same external metronome, has self-organization been demonstrated?

Answer: No. Synchronization may result from a shared external drive. To establish self-organization, we need to examine how interactions within the group produce order. This distinction also shows that the same macroscopic phenomenon can have more than one mechanism.

The Central Limit Theorem: Why Sums of Many Random Contributions Are Approximately Normal

A falling-ball apparatus illustrates a random walk: at each level, a ball moves randomly to the left or right, and its final position is the sum of many random displacements. The central limit theorem explains why suitably standardized sums often approach a normal distribution.

Distinguishing Random Variables, Distributions, and Moments

A random variable XXX assigns a numerical value to the outcome of a random experiment; xxx denotes one of its possible values. A continuous random variable is described by a probability density function (PDF), pX(x)p_X(x)pX​(x):

pX(x)≥0,∫−∞∞pX(x) dx=1,P(a≤X≤b)=∫abpX(x) dx.\begin{aligned} p_X(x)&\geq 0,\\ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p_X(x)\,dx&=1,\\ P(a\leq X\leq b)&=\int_a^b p_X(x)\,dx. \end{aligned} pX​(x)∫−∞∞​pX​(x)dxP(a≤X≤b)​≥0,=1,=∫ab​pX​(x)dx.​

The height of a density is not the probability of that exact value; a continuous distribution has P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0P(X=x)=0. A discrete random variable instead uses a probability mass function (PMF), pX(x)=P(X=x)p_X(x)=P(X=x)pX​(x)=P(X=x), and integration is replaced by summation over all possible values. For example, ∑xpX(x)=1\sum_xp_X(x)=1∑x​pX​(x)=1.

Mean, Variance, and Raw Moments

The mean describes location, the variance measures squared fluctuations around the mean, and the standard deviation σ\sigmaσ has the same units as XXX:

μ=E[X]=∫−∞∞xpX(x) dx,σ2=Var⁡(X)=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−(E[X])2.\begin{aligned} \mu&=E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x p_X(x)\,dx,\\ \sigma^2&=\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]\\ &=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2. \end{aligned} μσ2​=E[X]=∫−∞∞​xpX​(x)dx,=Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−(E[X])2.​

The kkkth raw moment is mk=E[Xk]m_k=E[X^k]mk​=E[Xk]. Therefore,

m0=1,μ=m1,σ2=m2−m12.m_0=1,\qquad \mu=m_1,\qquad \sigma^2=m_2-m_1^2. m0​=1,μ=m1​,σ2=m2​−m12​.

The second raw moment m2m_2m2​ equals the variance only when μ=0\mu=0μ=0. Do not confuse raw moments with central moments, E[(X−μ)k]E[(X-\mu)^k]E[(X−μ)k].

General and Standard Normal Distributions

A general normal, or Gaussian, distribution is written as X∼N(μ,σ2)X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)X∼N(μ,σ2). Its second parameter is the variance:

pX(x)=1σ2πexp⁡ ⁣[−(x−μ)22σ2],σ>0.p_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right],\qquad \sigma>0. pX​(x)=σ2π​1​exp[−2σ2(x−μ)2​],σ>0.

ϕ(z)=12πe−z2/2,E[Z]=0,Var⁡(Z)=1.\phi(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},\qquad E[Z]=0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(Z)=1. ϕ(z)=2π​1​e−z2/2,E[Z]=0,Var(Z)=1.

If X∼N(μ,σ2)X\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)X∼N(μ,σ2), then (X−μ)/σ∼N(0,1)(X-\mu)/\sigma\sim\mathcal N(0,1)(X−μ)/σ∼N(0,1). Define the standard normal cumulative distribution function by

Φ(z)=∫−∞zϕ(u) du.\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\phi(u)\,du. Φ(z)=∫−∞z​ϕ(u)du.

An interval probability is P(a≤Z≤b)=Φ(b)−Φ(a)P(a\leq Z\leq b)=\Phi(b)-\Phi(a)P(a≤Z≤b)=Φ(b)−Φ(a), and symmetry gives Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z)\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z).

The Precise CLT Statement and Its Assumptions

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), with

E[Xi]=μ finite,0<Var⁡(Xi)=σ2<∞.E[X_i]=\mu\ \text{finite},\qquad 0<\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty. E[Xi​]=μ finite,0<Var(Xi​)=σ2<∞.

“Identically distributed” means that all variables follow the same probability law; it does not mean that every observed value is identical. Independence means that the joint probability law factorizes: learning outcomes for any subset does not change the joint distribution of the remaining variables. Define the sum and sample mean as

Sn=∑i=1nXi,X‾n=Snn.S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \overline X_n=\frac{S_n}{n}. Sn​=i=1∑n​Xi​,Xn​=nSn​​.

The central limit theorem (CLT) states that the standardized sum converges in distribution:

Zn=Sn−nμσn=n(X‾n−μ)σ,Zn→dN(0,1),n→∞.\boxed{ \begin{aligned} Z_n&=\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n} =\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma},\\ Z_n&\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad n\to\infty. \end{aligned} } Zn​Zn​​=σn​Sn​−nμ​=σn​(Xn​−μ)​,d​N(0,1),n→∞.​​

Here, convergence in distribution means that P(Zn≤z)→Φ(z)P(Z_n\leq z)\to\Phi(z)P(Zn​≤z)→Φ(z) for every fixed real number zzz. The original variables XiX_iXi​ may be discrete or non-normal. The theorem does not assert exact normality at finite nnn, nor does it guarantee pointwise convergence of arbitrary probability densities.

Why Standardization Uses the Square Root of nnn

The scaling of means and variances explains the appearance of n\sqrt nn​:

E[Sn]=nμ,Var⁡(Sn)=nσ2,E[X‾n]=μ,Var⁡(X‾n)=σ2n.\begin{aligned} E[S_n]&=n\mu,\\ \operatorname{Var}(S_n)&=n\sigma^2,\\ E[\overline X_n]&=\mu,\\ \operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)&=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}. \end{aligned} E[Sn​]Var(Sn​)E[Xn​]Var(Xn​)​=nμ,=nσ2,=μ,=nσ2​.​

Independence makes the cross-covariances zero. The sum has standard deviation σn\sigma\sqrt nσn​, whereas the mean has standard deviation σ/n\sigma/\sqrt nσ/n​. For large nnn, we therefore often write the approximations

Sn≈N(nμ,nσ2),X‾n≈N ⁣(μ,σ2n).\begin{aligned} S_n&\approx\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2),\\ \overline X_n&\approx\mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). \end{aligned} Sn​Xn​​≈N(nμ,nσ2),≈N(μ,nσ2​).​

When μ=0,σ2=1\mu=0,\sigma^2=1μ=0,σ2=1, Zn=n X‾n=Sn/nZ_n=\sqrt n\,\overline X_n=S_n/\sqrt nZn​=n​Xn​=Sn​/n​; the square root covers only nnn. The fluctuations of the unstandardized mean shrink to zero as it approaches the constant μ\muμ; we must not write X‾n→N(0,1)\overline X_n\to\mathcal N(0,1)Xn​→N(0,1). A density approximation must also include the correct normalization factor:

pX‾n(x)≈nσ2πexp⁡ ⁣[−n(x−μ)22σ2].p_{\overline X_n}(x)\approx\frac{\sqrt n}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left[-\frac{n(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]. pXn​​(x)≈σ2π​n​​exp[−2σ2n(x−μ)2​].

Why the CLT Is Useful, and Why Its Assumptions Matter

Wealth, stock prices, earthquakes, and supermarket sales are influenced by many factors, which can motivate a normal model as an initial hypothesis. Before applying this reasoning, check whether the contributions add, whether they are independent, and whether the relevant distributional and finite-variance assumptions hold. The examples themselves do not prove that these quantities are normally distributed. Correlated interactions, multiplicative growth, or very heavy tails can invalidate this simple argument.

The version used here assumes i.i.d. variables with finite variance. Having equal means and variances alone does not imply identical distributions. More general CLTs can relax assumptions, but require additional theorems. There is also no universal threshold such as “n≥30n\geq30n≥30” that guarantees a reliable approximation for every distribution; skewness and heavy tails affect the rate of convergence.

Moment-Generating Functions: Encoding Moments in One Function

The moment-generating function (MGF) is

MX(t)=E[etX]=∫−∞∞etxpX(x) dx.M_X(t)=E[e^{tX}] =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{tx}p_X(x)\,dx. MX​(t)=E[etX]=∫−∞∞​etxpX​(x)dx.

For a discrete variable, use MX(t)=∑xetxpX(x)M_X(t)=\sum_x e^{tx}p_X(x)MX​(t)=∑x​etxpX​(x) instead.

Generating Moments by Differentiating at Zero

Expand etXe^{tX}etX around t=0t=0t=0. When summation and expectation can be interchanged,

etX=1+tX+t2X22!+t3X33!+⋯ ,MX(t)=1+m1t+m2t22!+m3t33!+⋯ .\begin{aligned} e^{tX}&=1+tX+\frac{t^2X^2}{2!}+\frac{t^3X^3}{3!}+\cdots,\\ M_X(t)&=1+m_1t+\frac{m_2t^2}{2!}+\frac{m_3t^3}{3!}+\cdots. \end{aligned} etXMX​(t)​=1+tX+2!t2X2​+3!t3X3​+⋯,=1+m1​t+2!m2​t2​+3!m3​t3​+⋯.​

Consequently,

MX(k)(0)=mk=E[Xk].\boxed{M_X^{(k)}(0)=m_k=E[X^k].} MX(k)​(0)=mk​=E[Xk].​

The notation MX(k)M_X^{(k)}MX(k)​ denotes the kkkth derivative, not the kkkth power of MXM_XMX​. Differentiate with respect to ttt first, then set t=0t=0t=0. Substituting t=0t=0t=0 directly into the MGF gives only MX(0)=1M_X(0)=1MX​(0)=1.

A sufficient condition for these standard MGF operations is that MX(t)M_X(t)MX​(t) be finite on an open neighborhood of 000. Not every distribution has such an MGF; even the existence of all raw moments does not automatically guarantee it. The usual finite-variance CLT does not require an MGF to exist; the MGF proof given here imposes an additional existence assumption.

Translation, Scaling, and Independent Sums

The proof below uses two rules:

MaX+b(t)=ebtMX(at),MX+Y(t)=MX(t)MY(t)(X,Y independent).\begin{aligned} M_{aX+b}(t)&=e^{bt}M_X(at),\\ M_{X+Y}(t)&=M_X(t)M_Y(t)\qquad (X,Y\ \text{independent}). \end{aligned} MaX+b​(t)MX+Y​(t)​=ebtMX​(at),=MX​(t)MY​(t)(X,Y independent).​

The first follows from et(aX+b)=ebteatXe^{t(aX+b)}=e^{bt}e^{atX}et(aX+b)=ebteatX. The second uses independence to obtain E[etXetY]=E[etX]E[etY]E[e^{tX}e^{tY}]=E[e^{tX}]E[e^{tY}]E[etXetY]=E[etX]E[etY]. Being merely uncorrelated is generally insufficient for the second rule.

The Standard Normal MGF: Complete the Square

Let Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1). Then

MZ(t)=∫−∞∞12πe−z2/2+tz dz=et2/2∫−∞∞12πe−(z−t)2/2 dz=et2/2.\begin{aligned} M_Z(t) &=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2+tz}\,dz\\ &=e^{t^2/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(z-t)^2/2}\,dz\\ &=\boxed{e^{t^2/2}}. \end{aligned} MZ​(t)​=∫−∞∞​2π​1​e−z2/2+tzdz=et2/2∫−∞∞​2π​1​e−(z−t)2/2dz=et2/2​.​

Distinguishing Raw Moments, Skewness, and Kurtosis

For a general distribution, skewness and kurtosis are defined as

γ1=E[(X−μ)3]σ3,β2=E[(X−μ)4]σ4,γ2=β2−3(excess kurtosis).\begin{aligned} \gamma_1&=\frac{E[(X-\mu)^3]}{\sigma^3},\\ \beta_2&=\frac{E[(X-\mu)^4]}{\sigma^4},\\ \gamma_2&=\beta_2-3\qquad\text{(excess kurtosis)}. \end{aligned} γ1​β2​γ2​​=σ3E[(X−μ)3]​,=σ4E[(X−μ)4]​,=β2​−3(excess kurtosis).​

The identities m3=γ1m_3=\gamma_1m3​=γ1​ and m4=β2m_4=\beta_2m4​=β2​ hold only for standardized variables. A normal distribution has skewness 000, kurtosis 333, and excess kurtosis 000; keep these three quantities distinct.

The MGF Proof of the CLT: Where Each Assumption Is Used

Consider the simplified case E[Xi]=0E[X_i]=0E[Xi​]=0, E[Xi2]=1E[X_i^2]=1E[Xi2​]=1, and assumes that the MGF of an individual XiX_iXi​ is finite near 000. The goal is to show that the MGF of Zn=Sn/nZ_n=S_n/\sqrt nZn​=Sn​/n​ converges to et2/2e^{t^2/2}et2/2.

This is precisely where independence and identical distributions enter the proof.

Step 3: Use a Second-Order Taylor Expansion at Zero

For fixed ttt, let u=t/n→0u=t/\sqrt n\to0u=t/n​→0. Since MX(0)=1M_X(0)=1MX​(0)=1, MX′(0)=0M'_X(0)=0MX′​(0)=0, and MX′′(0)=1M''_X(0)=1MX′′​(0)=1,

MX(u)=MX(0)+MX′(0)u+MX′′(0)2u2+o(u2)=1+u22+o(u2).\begin{aligned} M_X(u)&=M_X(0)+M'_X(0)u+\frac{M''_X(0)}{2}u^2+o(u^2)\\ &=1+\frac{u^2}{2}+o(u^2). \end{aligned} MX​(u)​=MX​(0)+MX′​(0)u+2MX′′​(0)​u2+o(u2)=1+2u2​+o(u2).​

Therefore,

MZn(t)=[1+t22n+o ⁣(1n)]n.M_{Z_n}(t)=\left[1+\frac{t^2}{2n}+o\!\left(\frac1n\right)\right]^n. MZn​​(t)=[1+2nt2​+o(n1​)]n.

The derivatives must be evaluated at the expansion point 000. At finite nnn, we cannot discard the remainder and retain an exact equality.

Step 4: Take the Limit

Using log⁡(1+v)=v+o(v)\log(1+v)=v+o(v)log(1+v)=v+o(v),

log⁡MZn(t)=nlog⁡ ⁣[1+t22n+o ⁣(1n)]⟶t22.\begin{aligned} \log M_{Z_n}(t) &=n\log\!\left[1+\frac{t^2}{2n}+o\!\left(\frac1n\right)\right]\\ &\longrightarrow\frac{t^2}{2}. \end{aligned} logMZn​​(t)​=nlog[1+2nt2​+o(n1​)]⟶2t2​.​

Hence MZn(t)→et2/2M_{Z_n}(t)\to e^{t^2/2}MZn​​(t)→et2/2. The continuity theorem for MGFs gives Zn→dN(0,1)Z_n\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1)Zn​d​N(0,1).

Step 5: Restore a General Mean and Variance

Repeat the argument for Yi=(Xi−μ)/σY_i=(X_i-\mu)/\sigmaYi​=(Xi​−μ)/σ. Since E[Yi]=0E[Y_i]=0E[Yi​]=0 and Var⁡(Yi)=1\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=1Var(Yi​)=1,

1n∑i=1nYi=Sn−nμσn→dN(0,1).\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i =\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1). n​1​i=1∑n​Yi​=σn​Sn​−nμ​d​N(0,1).

The complete chain is: standardize → turn the exponential of a sum into a product → factor by independence → use identical distributions → expand to second order at zero → apply (1+a/n)n→ea(1+a/n)^n\to e^a(1+a/n)n→ea. The finite mean determines the centering term, and the finite variance determines the scale.

Why the Finite-Variance CLT Is More General Than This Proof

We can instead use the characteristic function φX(t)=E[eitX]\varphi_X(t)=E[e^{itX}]φX​(t)=E[eitX], which always exists. For a variable with mean 000 and variance 111,

φX(u)=1−u22+o(u2),\varphi_X(u)=1-\frac{u^2}{2}+o(u^2), φX​(u)=1−2u2​+o(u2),

and the same argument gives

[φX ⁣(tn)]n→e−t2/2.\left[\varphi_X\!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt n}\right)\right]^n\to e^{-t^2/2}. [φX​(n​t​)]n→e−t2/2.

This explains how to address the gap caused by possible nonexistence of an MGF; the main derivation above still follows the MGF route.

Random Walks: From One Step to the Endpoint Distribution

Consider a walk in which each step is +1+1+1 to the right or −1-1−1 to the left, with probability 1/21/21/2 each. Steps are independent, and the position after nnn steps is Sn=X1+⋯+XnS_n=X_1+\cdots+X_nSn​=X1​+⋯+Xn​. Repeated left or right deflections in the falling-ball apparatus provide an intuitive analogy.

The Distribution and Moments of One Step

The step distribution is discrete, so it is described by a PMF:

P(X=1)=P(X=−1)=12,MX(t)=et+e−t2=cosh⁡t.P(X=1)=P(X=-1)=\frac12,\qquad M_X(t)=\frac{e^t+e^{-t}}{2}=\cosh t. P(X=1)=P(X=−1)=21​,MX​(t)=2et+e−t​=cosht.

Since cosh⁡′t=sinh⁡t\cosh' t=\sinh tcosh′t=sinht and sinh⁡′t=cosh⁡t\sinh' t=\cosh tsinh′t=cosht,

m1=0,m2=1,m3=0,m4=1.m_1=0,\quad m_2=1,\quad m_3=0,\quad m_4=1. m1​=0,m2​=1,m3​=0,m4​=1.

We can also see this directly: an odd power of XXX equals XXX, while an even power is always 111. A single step therefore has mean 000 and variance 111. Its distribution is not normal: its fourth moment is 111, whereas the fourth moment of a standard normal variable is 333.

The Exact Distribution After nnn Steps

Let KKK be the number of steps to the right. Then K∼Binomial⁡(n,1/2)K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/2)K∼Binomial(n,1/2) and Sn=K−(n−K)=2K−nS_n=K-(n-K)=2K-nSn​=K−(n−K)=2K−n, so

P(Sn=s)=2−n(n(n+s)/2),s=−n,−n+2,…,n.P(S_n=s)=2^{-n}\binom{n}{(n+s)/2},\qquad s=-n,-n+2,\ldots,n. P(Sn​=s)=2−n((n+s)/2n​),s=−n,−n+2,…,n.

All other values of sss have probability 000. The endpoint has the same parity as nnn. The MGF of SnS_nSn​ is (cosh⁡t)n(\cosh t)^n(cosht)n, and

E[Sn]=0,E[Sn2]=n,E[Sn3]=0,E[Sn4]=3n2−2n.\begin{aligned} E[S_n]&=0,\\ E[S_n^2]&=n,\\ E[S_n^3]&=0,\\ E[S_n^4]&=3n^2-2n. \end{aligned} E[Sn​]E[Sn2​]E[Sn3​]E[Sn4​]​=0,=n,=0,=3n2−2n.​

The fourth moment can also be derived by counting terms. In the expansion of (∑iXi)4(\sum_iX_i)^4(∑i​Xi​)4, the only terms with nonzero expectation are those containing one index four times, or two distinct indices twice each. Hence

E[Sn4]=nE[X4]+6(n2)(E[X2])2=n+3n(n−1)=3n2−2n.\begin{aligned} E[S_n^4]&=nE[X^4]+6\binom{n}{2}(E[X^2])^2\\ &=n+3n(n-1)\\ &=3n^2-2n. \end{aligned} E[Sn4​]​=nE[X4]+6(2n​)(E[X2])2=n+3n(n−1)=3n2−2n.​

The standardized endpoint Zn=Sn/nZ_n=S_n/\sqrt nZn​=Sn​/n​ has mean 000, variance 111, skewness 000, and kurtosis

E[Zn4]=3−2n⟶3.E[Z_n^4]=3-\frac2n\longrightarrow3. E[Zn4​]=3−n2​⟶3.

Its MGF is

MZn(t)=[cosh⁡ ⁣(tn)]n⟶et2/2.M_{Z_n}(t)=\left[\cosh\!\left(\frac{t}{\sqrt n}\right)\right]^n \longrightarrow e^{t^2/2}. MZn​​(t)=[cosh(n​t​)]n⟶et2/2.

Thus each step can have only two possible values while the standardized endpoint after many steps approaches a normal distribution.

Simulating the Random Walk and Interpreting the Results

Use n=5,25,125n=5,25,125n=5,25,125. For each nnn, perform 100010001000 independent repetitions. In each repetition, generate nnn equally likely ±1\pm1±1 steps and sum them, giving 100010001000 endpoints. Plot a histogram of the endpoints and compare it with N(0,n)\mathcal N(0,n)N(0,n); alternatively, plot Sn/nS_n/\sqrt nSn​/n​ and compare it with N(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1)N(0,1).

Number of steps nnn E[Sn]E[S_n]E[Sn​] SD⁡(Sn)\operatorname{SD}(S_n)SD(Sn​) Exact kurtosis of ZnZ_nZn​
5 0 5≈2.236\sqrt5\approx2.2365​≈2.236 2.6002.6002.600
25 0 555 2.9202.9202.920
125 0 125≈11.180\sqrt{125}\approx11.180125​≈11.180 2.9842.9842.984

Keep the following distinctions in mind when interpreting the results:

  • nnn is the number of steps in each walk, which determines the theoretical approximation. The 100010001000 repetitions are independent trials, which determine the sampling noise in the estimated histogram. Increasing the number of repetitions does not turn the true distribution of a fixed 555-step walk into a continuous normal distribution.
  • All three values of nnn are odd, and possible endpoints are separated by 222. Histogram bins of width 222, centered on the allowed endpoints, are appropriate. Normalize the histogram as a density when overlaying a PDF. If the bars instead show PMF values, compare them with the normal distribution’s probability areas over the corresponding intervals, rather than directly with density heights.
  • The theoretical parameters are μ=0,σ=n\mu=0,\sigma=\sqrt nμ=0,σ=n​. When fitting the simulated sample, report the sample mean and fitted standard deviation; these will generally differ slightly because of sampling fluctuations.
  • As nnn increases, the overall profile of the standardized endpoints generally becomes closer to a bell shape. At finite nnn, the true distribution remains discrete, and a finite set of 100010001000 simulations retains sampling noise.

Practice Questions and a General Solution Method

The following exercises combine probability, standardization, and moment-generating functions.

Question 1: Normal Approximations for a Sum and a Mean

Independent, identically distributed variables XiX_iXi​ have mean 101010 and standard deviation 222. Let n=100n=100n=100. Find the approximate distributions of SnS_nSn​ and X‾n\overline X_nXn​, and estimate P(9.6≤X‾n≤10.4)P(9.6\leq\overline X_n\leq10.4)P(9.6≤Xn​≤10.4).

Solution: First note that σ2=4\sigma^2=4σ2=4, so

S100≈N(1000,400),X‾100≈N(10,0.04).\begin{aligned} S_{100}&\approx\mathcal N(1000,400),\\ \overline X_{100}&\approx\mathcal N(10,0.04). \end{aligned} S100​X100​​≈N(1000,400),≈N(10,0.04).​

The standard deviation of the mean is 0.20.20.2, so the required probability is approximately Φ(2)−Φ(−2)≈0.9545\Phi(2)-\Phi(-2)\approx0.9545Φ(2)−Φ(−2)≈0.9545. Common errors are treating 0.040.040.04 as the standard deviation or incorrectly writing the variance of the sum as 1002×4100^2\times41002×4.

Question 2: Reading Moments from an MGF

Given MX(t)=exp⁡(3t+2t2)M_X(t)=\exp(3t+2t^2)MX​(t)=exp(3t+2t2), find the mean, variance, and second raw moment.

Solution: Comparing with the normal MGF exp⁡(μt+σ2t2/2)\exp(\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2)exp(μt+σ2t2/2) gives μ=3\mu=3μ=3 and σ2=4\sigma^2=4σ2=4. Therefore, m2=σ2+μ2=13m_2=\sigma^2+\mu^2=13m2​=σ2+μ2=13. Alternatively, differentiate to obtain MX′(0)=3M'_X(0)=3MX′​(0)=3 and MX′′(0)=13M''_X(0)=13MX′′​(0)=13; the latter is not the variance.

Question 3: An Exact Random-Walk Probability

What is the probability of reaching s=1s=1s=1 after 555 steps?

Solution: This requires K=(5+1)/2=3K=(5+1)/2=3K=(5+1)/2=3 rightward steps. Therefore,

P(S5=1)=(53)2−5=1032=516.P(S_5=1)=\binom{5}{3}2^{-5}=\frac{10}{32}=\frac5{16}. P(S5​=1)=(35​)2−5=3210​=165​.

Also, P(S5=0)=0P(S_5=0)=0P(S5​=0)=0, because an odd number of steps cannot lead to an even endpoint. A normal approximation cannot replace this restriction on the discrete support.

Question 4: Why Having Many Terms Is Not Enough

Suppose X1=⋯=Xn=YX_1=\cdots=X_n=YX1​=⋯=Xn​=Y, where E[Y]=0E[Y]=0E[Y]=0 and Var⁡(Y)=1\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1Var(Y)=1. Can the ordinary i.i.d. CLT establish Sn/n→N(0,1)S_n/\sqrt n\to\mathcal N(0,1)Sn​/n​→N(0,1)?

Solution: No. These variables are perfectly correlated, and Sn=nYS_n=nYSn​=nY. Thus Var⁡(Sn)=n2\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=n^2Var(Sn​)=n2 and Var⁡(Sn/n)=n\operatorname{Var}(S_n/\sqrt n)=nVar(Sn​/n​)=n; the independence assumption fails. Identical distributions do not imply independence, and the covariance terms cannot be dropped.

Question 5: Two Claims About the Proof

Are the following statements correct: “Finite variance guarantees that an MGF exists near 000” and “The MGF of the mean is [MX(t/n)]n[M_X(t/\sqrt n)]^n[MX​(t/n​)]n”?

Solution: Both are incorrect. The finite-variance CLT may hold even when the MGF method cannot be applied directly. The MGF of X‾n\overline X_nXn​ is [MX(t/n)]n[M_X(t/n)]^n[MX​(t/n)]n. When μ=0,σ=1\mu=0,\sigma=1μ=0,σ=1, the expression [MX(t/n)]n[M_X(t/\sqrt n)]^n[MX​(t/n​)]n instead corresponds to n X‾n\sqrt n\,\overline X_nn​Xn​.

A General Sequence for Calculations

  1. Identify the distribution of an individual variable and establish independence.
  2. Calculate μ,σ2\mu,\sigma^2μ,σ2.
  3. Determine whether the target is SnS_nSn​ or X‾n\overline X_nXn​.
  4. Calculate the mean and variance of that target.
  5. Standardize to ZZZ.
  6. Finish using Φ\PhiΦ, an exact discrete probability, or an MGF.

In an explanatory answer, state the theorem, its assumptions, and what a finite-sample approximation means.

Scale-Free Distributions: Stability, Power Laws, and Extreme Events

Stable distributions describe how a distribution can retain its shape under addition and rescaling. Power laws describe tails without a characteristic scale. Together, these ideas explain why a normal approximation may fail and how to calculate probabilities and moments for heavy-tailed variables.

Stable Distributions and Domains of Attraction: What Survives Addition?

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ be independent and identically distributed, and define

Sn=∑i=1nXi,Xˉn=Snn.S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \bar X_n=\frac{S_n}{n}. Sn​=i=1∑n​Xi​,Xˉn​=nSn​​.

A distribution is stable if addition preserves its shape up to a shift and a change of scale. More precisely, for every nnn, there are constants an>0,bn∈Ra_n>0,b_n\in\mathbb Ran​>0,bn​∈R such that

Sn=danX+bn.S_n\overset{d}{=}a_nX+b_n. Sn​=dan​X+bn​.

The symbol =d\overset{d}{=}=d means “equal in distribution”; it does not mean that the two sides take identical values in each realization. If one can choose bn=0b_n=0bn​=0, the distribution is strictly stable. Stability is an exact property for every finite nnn; attraction is a limiting property as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞. For example, the uniform distribution is not stable, but its standardized sums approach a normal distribution, so it belongs to the normal distribution's domain of attraction.

Stability of the Normal Distribution

If Xi∼N(μ,σ2)X_i\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\sigma^2)Xi​∼N(μ,σ2), then

MX(t)=E[etX]=exp⁡ ⁣(μt+σ2t22),MSn(t)=∏i=1nMXi(t)=exp⁡ ⁣(nμt+nσ2t22).\begin{aligned} M_X(t)&=\mathbb E[e^{tX}] =\exp\!\left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2t^2}{2}\right),\\ M_{S_n}(t)&=\prod_{i=1}^nM_{X_i}(t) =\exp\!\left(n\mu t+\frac{n\sigma^2t^2}{2}\right). \end{aligned} MX​(t)MSn​​(t)​=E[etX]=exp(μt+2σ2t2​),=i=1∏n​MXi​​(t)=exp(nμt+2nσ2t2​).​

Independence allows the expectation of a product to factor into the product of expectations. Therefore,

Sn∼N(nμ,nσ2),Xˉn∼N ⁣(μ,σ2n),Sn−nμσn∼N(0,1).\begin{aligned} S_n&\sim\mathcal N(n\mu,n\sigma^2),\\ \bar X_n&\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right),\\ \frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}&\sim\mathcal N(0,1). \end{aligned} Sn​Xˉn​σn​Sn​−nμ​​∼N(nμ,nσ2),∼N(μ,nσ2​),∼N(0,1).​

For a standard normal distribution, μ=0,σ=1\mu=0,\sigma=1μ=0,σ=1, the identity MSn(t)=MX(n t)M_{S_n}(t)=M_X(\sqrt n\,t)MSn​​(t)=MX​(n​t) holds. It shows that the width of the sum increases by a factor of n\sqrt nn​. The width of the sample mean decreases by a factor of 1/n1/\sqrt n1/n​.

Self-Similarity Must Include Density Normalization

If Sn=danXS_n\overset{d}{=}a_nXSn​=dan​X, then

fSn(s)=1anfX ⁣(san).f_{S_n}(s)=\frac1{a_n}f_X\!\left(\frac{s}{a_n}\right). fSn​​(s)=an​1​fX​(an​s​).

The factor 1/an1/a_n1/an​ comes from the change of variable and ensures that the density still integrates to 111. For standard normal summands,

fSn(s)=12πne−s2/(2n),fXˉn(x)=n2πe−nx2/2.\begin{aligned} f_{S_n}(s)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi n}}e^{-s^2/(2n)},\\ f_{\bar X_n}(x)&=\sqrt{\frac n{2\pi}}e^{-nx^2/2}. \end{aligned} fSn​​(s)fXˉn​​(x)​=2πn​1​e−s2/(2n),=2πn​​e−nx2/2.​

Common mistake: the expression p(n xˉ)p(\sqrt n\,\bar x)p(n​xˉ) illustrates rescaling the argument of a function. It cannot be used directly as the density of Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​, because that would omit the Jacobian. For nonnormal XiX_iXi​, the unstandardized sum SnS_nSn​ also generally does not converge to a fixed normal distribution: it must first be centered and rescaled.

Why Do Domains of Attraction Matter?

Macroscopic observations are often sums of many small contributions. If different microscopic distributions approach the same limit under the same rescaling, predicting the macroscopic shape does not require knowing every microscopic detail. This is the probabilistic starting point for universality. Independence, dependence, and tail conditions must still be checked.

How Can the Assumptions of the Central Limit Theorem Be Relaxed?

The ordinary i.i.d. version assumes E[Xi]=μ\mathbb E[X_i]=\muE[Xi​]=μ and 0<Var⁡(Xi)=σ2<∞0<\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty0<Var(Xi​)=σ2<∞, and concludes that

Sn−nμσn→dN(0,1).\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1). σn​Sn​−nμ​d​N(0,1).

The following three changes require separate consideration. “There are many terms” alone does not justify applying the CLT.

Nonidentical Distributions: The Lyapunov CLT

Suppose the XiX_iXi​ are independent but may have different means μi\mu_iμi​ and variances σi2\sigma_i^2σi2​. Define

sn2=∑i=1nσi2.s_n^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i^2. sn2​=i=1∑n​σi2​.

If there exists δ>0\delta>0δ>0 such that the Lyapunov condition holds,

lim⁡n→∞1sn2+δ∑i=1nE ⁣[∣Xi−μi∣2+δ]=0,\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{s_n^{2+\delta}} \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\!\left[|X_i-\mu_i|^{2+\delta}\right]=0, n→∞lim​sn2+δ​1​i=1∑n​E[∣Xi​−μi​∣2+δ]=0,

then

∑i=1n(Xi−μi)sn→dN(0,1).\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu_i)}{s_n}\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,1). sn​∑i=1n​(Xi​−μi​)​d​N(0,1).

The condition says that the aggregate contribution of large deviations, measured by a higher moment, becomes small relative to the overall fluctuation scale. It prevents a few terms from completely dominating the sum. Here sns_nsn​ is the standard deviation of the sum, not the sum of the individual standard deviations. The Lyapunov condition is sufficient, but it is not necessary for every possible CLT.

Example: Independent Bernoulli Variables with Different Parameters

Let the Xi∼Bernoulli⁡(pi)X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)Xi​∼Bernoulli(pi​) be independent, and suppose sn2≥cns_n^2\ge cnsn2​≥cn for some c>0c>0c>0. Choose δ=1\delta=1δ=1. Since ∣Xi−pi∣≤1|X_i-p_i|\le1∣Xi​−pi​∣≤1,

∑iE∣Xi−pi∣3sn3≤n(cn)3/2⟶0.\frac{\sum_i\mathbb E|X_i-p_i|^3}{s_n^3} \le\frac{n}{(cn)^{3/2}}\longrightarrow0. sn3​∑i​E∣Xi​−pi​∣3​≤(cn)3/2n​⟶0.

The standardized sum therefore approaches a normal distribution even when the pip_ipi​ differ. To answer such a question, write down the means, variances, and sns_nsn​; choose δ\deltaδ; bound the ratio; and state the limiting distribution.

Weak Dependence: The Coarse-Graining Intuition

If dependence persists only over short distances, grouping many observations into large blocks can make sufficiently separated blocks nearly independent, allowing a normal limit to survive. Condition: “small correlation” or “correlation tending to zero” alone is not sufficient to guarantee a CLT. Appropriate mixing or other dependence conditions are still needed. Being uncorrelated is also not the same as being independent.

For a stationary sequence, let C(k)=Cov⁡(Xt,Xt+k)C(k)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t+k})C(k)=Cov(Xt​,Xt+k​). Then the exact variance is

Var⁡(Sn)=nC(0)+2∑k=1n−1(n−k)C(k).\operatorname{Var}(S_n)=nC(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-k)C(k). Var(Sn​)=nC(0)+2k=1∑n−1​(n−k)C(k).

When the covariances are absolutely summable and suitable CLT conditions hold, one typically obtains

Var⁡(Sn)∼nσLR2,σLR2=C(0)+2∑k=1∞C(k)>0.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(S_n)&\sim n\sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2,\\ \sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2&=C(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}C(k)>0. \end{aligned} Var(Sn​)σLR2​​∼nσLR2​,=C(0)+2k=1∑∞​C(k)>0.​

The normalization must use the long-run variance σLR2\sigma_{\mathrm{LR}}^2σLR2​. Long-range dependence can change the n\sqrt nn​ scaling and may even change the limiting distribution.

Infinite Mean or Variance

The assumptions of the ordinary finite-variance CLT fail, so a normal approximation cannot be used automatically. The Cauchy distribution in the next section provides a concrete counterexample. More generally, normalized sums may approach a non-Gaussian stable distribution. However, “the assumptions of this theorem fail” does not mean that “every possible form of a normal limit is impossible.”

Cauchy / Lorentz: Averaging More Does Not Always Improve Accuracy

The Cauchy, or Lorentz, distribution centered at 000 with scale γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 has density

fX(x)=γπ(x2+γ2),−∞<x<∞.f_X(x)=\frac{\gamma}{\pi(x^2+\gamma^2)},\qquad -\infty<x<\infty. fX​(x)=π(x2+γ2)γ​,−∞<x<∞.

Its center is its median and mode, not its expectation. Normalization can be checked using
∫(x2+γ2)−1 dx=γ−1arctan⁡(x/γ)\int (x^2+\gamma^2)^{-1}\,dx=\gamma^{-1}\arctan(x/\gamma)∫(x2+γ2)−1dx=γ−1arctan(x/γ).

Why Does the Cauchy Mean Not Exist?

The positive and negative halves of the integral must be checked separately:

∫0RxfX(x) dx=γ2πlog⁡ ⁣(R2+γ2γ2)→R→∞+∞.\int_0^R x f_X(x)\,dx =\frac{\gamma}{2\pi}\log\!\left(\frac{R^2+\gamma^2}{\gamma^2}\right) \xrightarrow{R\to\infty}+\infty. ∫0R​xfX​(x)dx=2πγ​log(γ2R2+γ2​)R→∞​+∞.

The negative half-line contributes −∞-\infty−∞, so the ordinary expectation is the undefined expression ∞−∞\infty-\infty∞−∞. The symmetric principal value
lim⁡R→∞∫−RRxfX(x) dx=0\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{-R}^{R}xf_X(x)\,dx=0limR→∞​∫−RR​xfX​(x)dx=0 does not establish the existence of the expectation. Also, x2fX(x)→γ/πx^2f_X(x)\to\gamma/\pix2fX​(x)→γ/π, so E[X2]=∞\mathbb E[X^2]=\inftyE[X2]=∞. The logarithmic antiderivative has coefficient γ/(2π)\gamma/(2\pi)γ/(2π).

Why Switch to the Characteristic Function?

For this distribution, the moment-generating function MX(t)=E[etX]M_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX}]MX​(t)=E[etX] diverges at every nonzero real ttt. The characteristic function always exists, because ∣eiqX∣=1|e^{iqX}|=1∣eiqX∣=1:

φX(q)=E[eiqX]=∫−∞∞fX(x)eiqx dx,fX(x)=12π∫−∞∞φX(q)e−iqx dq.\begin{aligned} \varphi_X(q)&=\mathbb E[e^{iqX}] =\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_X(x)e^{iqx}\,dx,\\ f_X(x)&=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\varphi_X(q)e^{-iqx}\,dq. \end{aligned} φX​(q)fX​(x)​=E[eiqX]=∫−∞∞​fX​(x)eiqxdx,=2π1​∫−∞∞​φX​(q)e−iqxdq.​

The inversion formula requires appropriate integrability conditions. Those conditions hold here because the Cauchy characteristic function is integrable. The forward and inverse Fourier transforms use opposite signs, with a factor 1/(2π)1/(2\pi)1/(2π) in the inverse transform.

For the Cauchy distribution, φX(q)=e−γ∣q∣\varphi_X(q)=e^{-\gamma|q|}φX​(q)=e−γ∣q∣. Verification: the inverse transform gives an elementary check without requiring contour integration:

12π∫−∞∞e−γ∣q∣e−iqx dq=1π∫0∞e−γqcos⁡(qx) dq=1πRe⁡1γ+ix=γπ(γ2+x2).\begin{aligned} &\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\gamma|q|}e^{-iqx}\,dq\\ &\quad=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-\gamma q}\cos(qx)\,dq\\ &\quad=\frac1\pi\operatorname{Re}\frac1{\gamma+ix} =\frac{\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+x^2)}. \end{aligned} ​2π1​∫−∞∞​e−γ∣q∣e−iqxdq=π1​∫0∞​e−γqcos(qx)dq=π1​Reγ+ix1​=π(γ2+x2)γ​.​

The Key Calculation for Independent Sums

φSn(q)=[φX(q)]n=e−nγ∣q∣,⟹fSn(s)=nγπ[s2+(nγ)2].\begin{aligned} \varphi_{S_n}(q)&=[\varphi_X(q)]^n=e^{-n\gamma|q|},\\ \Longrightarrow\quad f_{S_n}(s)&=\frac{n\gamma}{\pi[s^2+(n\gamma)^2]}. \end{aligned} φSn​​(q)⟹fSn​​(s)​=[φX​(q)]n=e−nγ∣q∣,=π[s2+(nγ)2]nγ​.​

Thus Sn∼Cauchy⁡(0,nγ)S_n\sim\operatorname{Cauchy}(0,n\gamma)Sn​∼Cauchy(0,nγ), whereas

φXˉn(q)=φSn(q/n)=e−γ∣q∣,Xˉn=dX1.\begin{aligned} \varphi_{\bar X_n}(q)&=\varphi_{S_n}(q/n)=e^{-\gamma|q|},\\ &\boxed{\bar X_n\overset{d}{=}X_1}. \end{aligned} φXˉn​​(q)​=φSn​​(q/n)=e−γ∣q∣,Xˉn​=dX1​​.​

The width of the sample-mean distribution does not shrink with sample size. For example, whatever the value of nnn, Pr⁡(∣Xˉn∣>γ)=1/2\Pr(|\bar X_n|>\gamma)=1/2Pr(∣Xˉn​∣>γ)=1/2. This does not contradict the usual law of large numbers, because the Cauchy distribution does not satisfy the sufficient condition of a finite first absolute moment.

Lévy Stable Distributions, the Generalized CLT, and Scaling Exponents

A symmetric stable family centered at zero has characteristic function

φX(q)=exp⁡(−γ∣q∣α),γ>0,0<α≤2.\boxed{\varphi_X(q)=\exp(-\gamma|q|^\alpha)}, \qquad \gamma>0,\quad 0<\alpha\le2. φX​(q)=exp(−γ∣q∣α)​,γ>0,0<α≤2.

Here α\alphaα is the stability index, also associated with the tail exponent, while γ\gammaγ controls scale and has the same physical dimensions as XαX^\alphaXα. In this stable-family formula, γ\gammaγ is a scale parameter, distinct from its use for a density-tail exponent. A location parameter of zero does not imply that the mean exists: a symmetric stable distribution has no finite mean when α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1. General stable distributions may also have location and skewness parameters.

Independence and uniqueness of characteristic functions give

φSn(q)=e−nγ∣q∣α=φX(n1/αq)⟹Sn=dn1/αX.\varphi_{S_n}(q)=e^{-n\gamma|q|^\alpha} =\varphi_X(n^{1/\alpha}q) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_n\overset{d}{=}n^{1/\alpha}X. φSn​​(q)=e−nγ∣q∣α=φX​(n1/αq)⟹Sn​=dn1/αX.

The density and sample mean therefore scale as

fSn(s)=n−1/αfX(s/n1/α),Xˉn=dn1/α−1X.\begin{aligned} f_{S_n}(s)&=n^{-1/\alpha}f_X(s/n^{1/\alpha}),\\ \bar X_n&\overset{d}{=}n^{1/\alpha-1}X. \end{aligned} fSn​​(s)Xˉn​​=n−1/αfX​(s/n1/α),=dn1/α−1X.​

This derivation explains three important cases:

  • α=2\alpha=2α=2: the normal distribution. Comparing e−γq2e^{-\gamma q^2}e−γq2 with the normal characteristic function gives σ2=2γ\sigma^2=2\gammaσ2=2γ. The width of the sample mean decreases as n−1/2n^{-1/2}n−1/2.
  • α=1\alpha=1α=1: the Cauchy distribution. The sum scales by nnn, while the scale of the sample mean remains unchanged.
  • 1<α<21<\alpha<21<α<2: the mean exists, but the fluctuation scale of the sample mean decreases as n−(1−1/α)n^{-(1-1/\alpha)}n−(1−1/α), more slowly than in the normal case. For 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1, this scale instead increases.

Here “width” may be measured by a quantile-based scale such as the interquartile range. It cannot mean a standard deviation that does not exist. For example, with α=3/2\alpha=3/2α=3/2, the scale of SnS_nSn​ is n2/3n^{2/3}n2/3 and that of Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​ is n−1/3n^{-1/3}n−1/3.

Power-Law Tails and Moments

Symmetric non-Gaussian stable distributions satisfy

fX(x)∼Cα∣x∣−1−α(∣x∣→∞),0<α<2,f_X(x)\sim C_\alpha |x|^{-1-\alpha}\quad (|x|\to\infty), \qquad 0<\alpha<2, fX​(x)∼Cα​∣x∣−1−α(∣x∣→∞),0<α<2,

and, for r>0r>0r>0, E∣X∣r<∞\mathbb E|X|^r<\inftyE∣X∣r<∞ if and only if r<αr<\alphar<α. Thus every non-Gaussian stable distribution has a divergent second moment. In the symmetric case, a finite mean exists only when α>1\alpha>1α>1. Important endpoint: when α=2\alpha=2α=2, the tail is Gaussian. Substituting α=2\alpha=2α=2 into the non-Gaussian power-law expression to obtain ∣x∣−3|x|^{-3}∣x∣−3 is incorrect. The normal distribution has finite absolute moments of every order.

The Generalized Central Limit Theorem

If the tails of i.i.d. random variables place them in the domain of attraction of a stable distribution, constants an>0,bna_n>0,b_nan​>0,bn​ can be chosen so that

Sn−bnan→dZα.\frac{S_n-b_n}{a_n}\xrightarrow{d}Z_\alpha. an​Sn​−bn​​d​Zα​.

For regular power-law tails with index α∈(0,2)\alpha\in(0,2)α∈(0,2), the typical growth of ana_nan​ is n1/αn^{1/\alpha}n1/α, possibly accompanied by a slowly varying factor in more general cases. When α>1\alpha>1α>1, the usual centering is bn=nE[X]b_n=n\mathbb E[X]bn​=nE[X]. The earlier equality for every finite nnn applies to exactly symmetric stable distributions.

Stable Distributions and Other Distribution Families

“Stable distributions are either normal or have power-law tails” describes the stable family. It cannot be extended to “all observations of complex systems must be normal or power-law distributed.” Empirical distributions may also have exponential tails, lognormal tails, mixture shapes, or finite cutoffs. The reverse claim, “every power-law distribution is strictly stable,” is also false: the Pareto distribution is generally not stable, although for suitable tail indices it can belong to a stable domain of attraction.

Calculating with Power Laws: Exponents, Tail Probabilities, and Moments

To avoid an off-by-one error in the exponent, write

fX(x)=Cx−τ,τ=1+α,x≥xmin⁡>0.f_X(x)=C x^{-\tau},\qquad \tau=1+\alpha, \qquad x\ge x_{\min}>0. fX​(x)=Cx−τ,τ=1+α,x≥xmin​>0.

Here τ\tauτ is the density exponent, while α\alphaα is the cumulative-tail exponent. For τ>1\tau>1τ>1, normalization gives

1=C∫xmin⁡∞x−τ dx=Cxmin⁡1−ττ−1,⟹C=(τ−1)xmin⁡τ−1.\begin{aligned} 1&=C\int_{x_{\min}}^\infty x^{-\tau}\,dx =\frac{C x_{\min}^{1-\tau}}{\tau-1},\\ \Longrightarrow\quad C&=(\tau-1)x_{\min}^{\tau-1}. \end{aligned} 1⟹C​=C∫xmin​∞​x−τdx=τ−1Cxmin1−τ​​,=(τ−1)xminτ−1​.​

A pure power law cannot be integrable at both ends of the entire interval (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞). A lower cutoff or another modification at small scales is therefore essential.

What Does “Scale-Free” Mean?

Within the range where the power law holds,

fX(cx)=c−τfX(x),Pr⁡(X>cx)Pr⁡(X>x)=c−α(c≥1).f_X(cx)=c^{-\tau}f_X(x),\qquad \frac{\Pr(X>cx)}{\Pr(X>x)}=c^{-\alpha}\quad(c\ge1). fX​(cx)=c−τfX​(x),Pr(X>x)Pr(X>cx)​=c−α(c≥1).

Multiplying the threshold by a fixed factor produces the same relative reduction in probability, regardless of the starting value xxx. The tail has no single exponential decay scale of the kind found in e−x/x0e^{-x/x_0}e−x/x0​. This does not mean that the distribution has no scale parameters at all, or that its mean must fail to exist. The Pareto lower cutoff xmin⁡x_{\min}xmin​, a stable distribution's scale parameter, and quantile-based widths can all exist.

From the Density to the Complementary CDF

F‾X(x)=Pr⁡(X>x)=∫x∞Cu−τ du=Cτ−1x−(τ−1)∝x−α.\begin{aligned} \overline F_X(x)&=\Pr(X>x)=\int_x^\infty Cu^{-\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{C}{\tau-1}x^{-(\tau-1)}\propto x^{-\alpha}. \end{aligned} FX​(x)​=Pr(X>x)=∫x∞​Cu−τdu=τ−1C​x−(τ−1)∝x−α.​

Consequently, on logarithmic axes,

log⁡fX(x)=log⁡C−τlog⁡x,log⁡F‾X(x)=const−αlog⁡x.\begin{aligned} \log f_X(x)&=\log C-\tau\log x,\\ \log\overline F_X(x)&=\mathrm{const}-\alpha\log x. \end{aligned} logfX​(x)logFX​(x)​=logC−τlogx,=const−αlogx.​

The PDF slope is −(1+α)-(1+\alpha)−(1+α); the CCDF slope is −α-\alpha−α; the CDF F=1−F‾F=1-\overline FF=1−F itself is generally not a straight line. Identify the vertical-axis quantity before reading off an exponent. With logarithmic binning, raw bin counts also include the bin width, which increases with xxx; divide by bin width to estimate a density. A straight line is a diagnostic clue for a power law, but approximate linearity over a finite range is not a rigorous proof.

One Integral Gives the Moment Condition

For r>0r>0r>0,

E[Xr]=C∫xmin⁡∞xr−τ dx<∞⟺r−τ<−1⟺r<τ−1=α.\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[X^r]&=C\int_{x_{\min}}^\infty x^{r-\tau}\,dx<\infty\\ &\Longleftrightarrow r-\tau<-1\\ &\Longleftrightarrow \boxed{r<\tau-1=\alpha}. \end{aligned} E[Xr]​=C∫xmin​∞​xr−τdx<∞⟺r−τ<−1⟺r<τ−1=α​.​

At r=αr=\alphar=α, the integral is of the form ∫dx/x\int dx/x∫dx/x, which diverges logarithmically; equality does not count as finite. A finite mean therefore requires α>1\alpha>1α>1, and a finite second moment and variance require α>2\alpha>2α>2. For a positive random variable with α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1, the expectation is +∞+\infty+∞. For a symmetric distribution with two heavy tails, the mean may instead be undefined. These are different statements.

Finite-System Cutoffs

If xmin⁡≤X≤xmax⁡<∞x_{\min}\le X\le x_{\max}<\inftyxmin​≤X≤xmax​<∞, all positive-order moments are finite, even though a broad intermediate range may still follow a power law. For f(x)=Cx−1−αf(x)=C x^{-1-\alpha}f(x)=Cx−1−α,

E[Xr]={Cr−α(xmax⁡r−α−xmin⁡r−α),r≠α,Clog⁡(xmax⁡/xmin⁡),r=α.\mathbb E[X^r]= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{C}{r-\alpha}\left(x_{\max}^{r-\alpha}-x_{\min}^{r-\alpha}\right),&r\ne\alpha,\\[4pt] \displaystyle C\log(x_{\max}/x_{\min}),&r=\alpha. \end{cases} E[Xr]=⎩⎪⎨⎪⎧​r−αC​(xmaxr−α​−xminr−α​),Clog(xmax​/xmin​),​r=α,r=α.​

Thus a cutoff removes mathematically infinite moments, but their estimated values can remain highly sensitive to the upper limit and to extreme observations.

Pareto Wealth Distributions and Microscopic Exchange Models

The Pareto model has parameters α>0,xm>0\alpha>0,x_m>0α>0,xm​>0:

fX(x)={αxmαxα+1,x≥xm,0,x<xm,FX(x)={1−(xm/x)α,x≥xm,0,x<xm.\begin{aligned} f_X(x)&=\begin{cases} \dfrac{\alpha x_m^\alpha}{x^{\alpha+1}},&x\ge x_m,\\ 0,&x<x_m, \end{cases}\\ F_X(x)&=\begin{cases} 1-(x_m/x)^\alpha,&x\ge x_m,\\ 0,&x<x_m. \end{cases} \end{aligned} fX​(x)FX​(x)​=⎩⎪⎨⎪⎧​xα+1αxmα​​,0,​x≥xm​,x<xm​,​={1−(xm​/x)α,0,​x≥xm​,x<xm​.​​

For x≥xmx\ge x_mx≥xm​, the CDF follows by integrating ∫xmxfX(u) du\int_{x_m}^{x}f_X(u)\,du∫xm​x​fX​(u)du, and the tail probability is (xm/x)α(x_m/x)^\alpha(xm​/x)α. For any r<αr<\alphar<α, the moment is

E[Xr]=αxmrα−r.\mathbb E[X^r]=\frac{\alpha x_m^r}{\alpha-r}. E[Xr]=α−rαxmr​​.

The mean, median, and variance are

E[X]=αxmα−1(α>1),Med⁡(X)=xm21/α,Q(u)=xm(1−u)−1/α(0<u<1),Var⁡(X)=αxm2(α−1)2(α−2)(α>2).\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[X]&=\frac{\alpha x_m}{\alpha-1}\quad(\alpha>1),\\ \operatorname{Med}(X)&=x_m2^{1/\alpha},\\ Q(u)&=x_m(1-u)^{-1/\alpha}\quad(0<u<1),\\ \operatorname{Var}(X)&=\frac{\alpha x_m^2}{(\alpha-1)^2(\alpha-2)}\quad(\alpha>2). \end{aligned} E[X]Med(X)Q(u)Var(X)​=α−1αxm​​(α>1),=xm​21/α,=xm​(1−u)−1/α(0<u<1),=(α−1)2(α−2)αxm2​​(α>2).​

The final expression follows by simplifying E[X2]−(E[X])2\mathbb E[X^2]-(\mathbb E[X])^2E[X2]−(E[X])2. Do not substitute α≤2\alpha\le2α≤2 into this formula and interpret a negative result as a “variance.” For 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2, the variance is infinite. For α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1, a finite mean already fails to exist.

The Gini Coefficient and Lorenz Curve

Assume α>1\alpha>1α>1. Let uuu be the cumulative population share counted from the poorest individuals upward. The Lorenz curve L(u)L(u)L(u) gives the share of wealth held by those individuals:

L(u)=∫0uQ(v) dvE[X]=1−(1−u)(α−1)/α.L(u)=\frac{\int_0^u Q(v)\,dv}{\mathbb E[X]} =1-(1-u)^{(\alpha-1)/\alpha}. L(u)=E[X]∫0u​Q(v)dv​=1−(1−u)(α−1)/α.

Under perfect equality, L(u)=uL(u)=uL(u)=u. The Gini coefficient is twice the area between the equality line and the Lorenz curve:

G=1−2∫01L(u) du=12α−1.G=1-2\int_0^1L(u)\,du=\boxed{\frac1{2\alpha-1}}. G=1−2∫01​L(u)du=2α−11​​.

A smaller α\alphaα means a heavier tail and greater concentration of wealth. For an ideal Pareto distribution with α≤1\alpha\le1α≤1, the population Gini coefficient cannot be calculated directly from this finite-mean definition.

Worked Example: A Pareto Distribution with α=1.5\alpha=1.5α=1.5

Take α=1.5,xm=1\alpha=1.5,x_m=1α=1.5,xm​=1. Then

F(x)=1−x−3/2,Pr⁡(X>4)=4−3/2=18,E[X]=3,Med⁡(X)=22/3≈1.587,G=12.\begin{aligned} F(x)&=1-x^{-3/2},\\ \Pr(X>4)&=4^{-3/2}=\frac18,\\ \mathbb E[X]&=3,\\ \operatorname{Med}(X)&=2^{2/3}\approx1.587,\\ G&=\frac12. \end{aligned} F(x)Pr(X>4)E[X]Med(X)G​=1−x−3/2,=4−3/2=81​,=3,=22/3≈1.587,=21​.​

The second moment and variance diverge, while the mean remains finite. The density has log-log slope −2.5-2.5−2.5, and the CCDF has slope −1.5-1.5−1.5. Interpretation: α≈1.5\alpha\approx1.5α≈1.5 is one possible model of a heavy wealth tail. It does not imply that all countries, periods, or wealth ranges follow exactly this distribution. A finite sample also cannot prove that the true population variance of wealth is infinite.

Why Consider an Agent-Based Model?

Wealth-exchange models describe how trading and saving rules generate a distribution of wealth across individuals. When two individuals i,ji,ji,j are selected,

xi′=xi−Δx,xj′=xj+Δx,xi′+xj′=xi+xj.x_i'=x_i-\Delta x,\qquad x_j'=x_j+\Delta x, \qquad x_i'+x_j'=x_i+x_j. xi′​=xi​−Δx,xj′​=xj​+Δx,xi′​+xj′​=xi​+xj​.

This closed model conserves total wealth, much as colliding molecules exchange energy. A simulation must also constrain its trading rules so that it does not inadvertently produce wealth values that the model forbids, such as negative wealth. Conservation alone does not imply a power law: the exchange and saving rules determine the eventual distribution.

Kinetic theory and wealth exchange have the following correspondence:

Kinetic theory of gases Wealth-exchange model
Particles Individuals or agents
Kinetic energy KKK Wealth xxx
Collisions Trades
Geometric dimension DDD Effective parameter DλD_\lambdaDλ​

The corresponding temperature scales are

kBT=2⟨K⟩D↔Tλ=2⟨x⟩Dλ.k_BT=\frac{2\langle K\rangle}{D} \quad\leftrightarrow\quad T_\lambda=\frac{2\langle x\rangle}{D_\lambda}. kB​T=D2⟨K⟩​↔Tλ​=Dλ​2⟨x⟩​.

The dimensionless variables are K/(kBT)K/(k_BT)K/(kB​T) and x/Tλx/T_\lambdax/Tλ​, respectively. A Gamma-distribution shape function may be written γD/2\gamma_{D/2}γD/2​; it is distinct from the stable-distribution scale parameter γ\gammaγ. Simple exchange rules can generate population-level statistics with an approximately Gibbs-like body and a Pareto-like upper tail.

Earthquakes and Aftershocks: Identify the Variable Before Calling It a Power Law

Earthquake magnitude, amplitude, cumulative event counts, and probability densities are different quantities. Distinguishing them is essential because a change of variable changes the tail exponent and can change whether the mean is finite.

The Gutenberg–Richter Law

For a fixed region, observation period, and completeness threshold m0m_0m0​, the cumulative number of earthquakes satisfies

log⁡10N(M≥m)=a−bm,b≈1 as an illustrative value.\log_{10}N(M\ge m)=a-bm,\qquad b\approx1\text{ as an illustrative value}. log10​N(M≥m)=a−bm,b≈1 as an illustrative value.

Normalizing within the set of events with M≥m0M\ge m_0M≥m0​ gives

Pr⁡(M≥m∣M≥m0)=10−b(m−m0),m≥m0.\Pr(M\ge m\mid M\ge m_0)=10^{-b(m-m_0)},\qquad m\ge m_0. Pr(M≥m∣M≥m0​)=10−b(m−m0​),m≥m0​.

The magnitude density and mean are therefore

fM(m)=bln⁡10 10−b(m−m0),E[M]=m0+1bln⁡10<∞.\begin{aligned} f_M(m)&=b\ln10\,10^{-b(m-m_0)},\\ \mathbb E[M]&=m_0+\frac1{b\ln10}<\infty. \end{aligned} fM​(m)E[M]​=bln1010−b(m−m0​),=m0​+bln101​<∞.​

The tail of magnitude MMM is exponential, not a power law. For b>0b>0b>0 and a finite lower threshold, this magnitude distribution has a finite mean.

Using the simplified relation M−m0=log⁡10(A/A0)M-m_0=\log_{10}(A/A_0)M−m0​=log10​(A/A0​), the amplitude AAA instead satisfies

Pr⁡(A>a)=(A0a)b,fA(a)=bA0ba−b−1,a≥A0.\begin{aligned} \Pr(A>a)&=\left(\frac{A_0}{a}\right)^b,\\ f_A(a)&=bA_0^b a^{-b-1},\qquad a\ge A_0. \end{aligned} Pr(A>a)fA​(a)​=(aA0​​)b,=bA0b​a−b−1,a≥A0​.​

The same result follows from fA(a)=fM(m(a))∣dm/da∣f_A(a)=f_M(m(a))|dm/da|fA​(a)=fM​(m(a))∣dm/da∣, where ∣dm/da∣=1/(aln⁡10)|dm/da|=1/(a\ln10)∣dm/da∣=1/(aln10). Omitting this Jacobian changes the power-law exponent by one. The amplitude-tail index is α=b\alpha=bα=b. In the ideal untruncated case with b=1b=1b=1, the amplitude mean diverges, while the magnitude mean remains finite. Actual magnitude definitions also include instrumental, distance, and other corrections, so M=log⁡10AM=\log_{10}AM=log10​A is not a complete measurement formula.

The meaning of the cumulative count can be checked against the USGS description of the Gutenberg–Richter law. The probability transformation and mean above then follow directly from the equations.

Omori's Law for Aftershocks

An aftershock decay law Nt∼t−pN_t\sim t^{-p}Nt​∼t−p, with p≈1p\approx1p≈1, describes the event rate per unit time. A commonly used regularized form is

r(t)=K(t+c)p,K>0, c>0,r(t)=\frac{K}{(t+c)^p},\qquad K>0,\ c>0, r(t)=(t+c)pK​,K>0, c>0,

where ccc removes the singularity at t=0t=0t=0. When p=1p=1p=1, the expected event count over [t1,t2][t_1,t_2][t1​,t2​] is

E[N(t1,t2)]=∫t1t2r(t) dt=Kln⁡ ⁣t2+ct1+c.\mathbb E[N(t_1,t_2)]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}r(t)\,dt =K\ln\!\frac{t_2+c}{t_1+c}. E[N(t1​,t2​)]=∫t1​t2​​r(t)dt=Klnt1​+ct2​+c​.

A rate is not a normalized probability density. The relation r(t)∝1/tr(t)\propto1/tr(t)∝1/t alone does not establish that “the mean aftershock time is infinite, so aftershocks never stop.” If a separate probability model is defined by fT(t)∝t−pf_T(t)\propto t^{-p}fT​(t)∝t−p for t≥tmin⁡>0t\ge t_{\min}>0t≥tmin​>0, normalization requires p>1p>1p>1, and a finite mean requires p>2p>2p>2. With p=1p=1p=1, a model over an infinite time interval cannot even be normalized. This is another reason to handle exponent boundaries carefully.

Consequences of Having No Characteristic Scale

The St Petersburg paradox. The first head of a fair coin appears on toss nnn, where n=1,2,…n=1,2,\ldotsn=1,2,…, and the payout is W=2n−1W=2^{n-1}W=2n−1. Then

Pr⁡(N=n)=2−n,E[W]=∑n=1∞2n−12−n=∑n=1∞12=∞.\begin{aligned} \Pr(N=n)&=2^{-n},\\ \mathbb E[W]&=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{n-1}2^{-n} =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac12=\infty. \end{aligned} Pr(N=n)E[W]​=2−n,=n=1∑∞​2n−12−n=n=1∑∞​21​=∞.​

Nevertheless, Pr⁡(W<∞)=1\Pr(W<\infty)=1Pr(W<∞)=1: a finite outcome almost surely is entirely consistent with an infinite expectation. For example, Pr⁡(W≤2)=3/4\Pr(W\le2)=3/4Pr(W≤2)=3/4. Pricing only by risk-neutral expected break-even value gives no finite fair entry fee. Wealth limits, payout caps, risk preferences, or utility functions change the pricing problem. If NNN is the toss on which the first head occurs, the number of preceding tails is N−1N-1N−1; consistent indexing is essential.

Extreme events are not automatically outliers to discard. A heavy-tailed distribution assigns much greater probabilities to large events than a Gaussian model does. If very large and small events arise from the same mechanism, removing the largest observations simply because of their size systematically underestimates tail risk. Biological extinctions and large market crashes illustrate extreme events. In financial models, option prices can be sensitive to distribution tails and volatility. The methodological lesson is: check data quality and the generating mechanism before deciding that a point is anomalous; “rare” is not equivalent to “bad data.” A single histogram or market crash does not rigorously establish an exact power law for the entire tail.

Econophysics: returns, memory, and volatility. The efficient-market hypothesis, Brownian motion, normality of returns, existence of variance, and short or long memory are distinct questions. The efficient-market hypothesis does not itself imply normally distributed returns. GARCH is a family of models for a conditional variance that changes over time, allowing volatility clustering: large fluctuations tend to be followed by further large fluctuations. A volatility smile describes implied volatility, inferred through the same underlying pricing model, varying with strike price.

Structures across scales and the motivation for modeling. Cosmic superstructures raise questions about patterns across scales. Avalanche distributions in systems of coupled pendulums show how local interactions can generate a population-level power law. Simple mechanisms can therefore explain collective phenomena and statistical patterns without predicting every individual catastrophe. A power law alone does not uniquely identify the microscopic mechanism.

Self-Test

Check whether you can solve the following questions independently.

  1. Let f(x)=Cx−5/2f(x)=Cx^{-5/2}f(x)=Cx−5/2 for x≥1x\ge1x≥1. Find CCC and the CCDF, and determine whether the mean and variance are finite.

    Answer: C=3/2C=3/2C=3/2, Pr⁡(X>x)=x−3/2\Pr(X>x)=x^{-3/2}Pr(X>x)=x−3/2, and E[X]=3\mathbb E[X]=3E[X]=3. The variance diverges.

  2. An empirical CCDF has log-log slope −0.8-0.8−0.8. What is the density-tail exponent? Does the mean of the positive random variable exist?

    Answer: α=0.8\alpha=0.8α=0.8 and τ=1.8\tau=1.8τ=1.8. Under the ideal infinite-tail model, the mean is +∞+\infty+∞.

  3. Let XiX_iXi​ be independent standard Cauchy variables, with n=100n=100n=100. What are the scales of SnS_nSn​ and Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​?

    Answer: 100100100 and 111, respectively. The formula σ/n\sigma/\sqrt nσ/n​ does not apply.

  4. A symmetric stable distribution has index α=1.5\alpha=1.5α=1.5. If the sample size increases from nnn to 8n8n8n, how does the typical width of the sample mean change?

    Answer: it is multiplied by 81/1.5−1=8−1/3=1/28^{1/1.5-1}=8^{-1/3}=1/281/1.5−1=8−1/3=1/2. There is no finite standard deviation to rescale in this way.

  5. Does N(M≥m)∝10−mN(M\ge m)\propto10^{-m}N(M≥m)∝10−m mean that the magnitude density is proportional to M−1M^{-1}M−1?

    Answer: no. MMM is a shifted exponential variable. If M=log⁡10A+constantM=\log_{10}A+\text{constant}M=log10​A+constant, the amplitude CCDF is proportional to A−1A^{-1}A−1 and its density to A−2A^{-2}A−2.

Problem-solving sequence: define the random variable and its support; identify whether the given quantity is a PDF, CDF, CCDF, or event rate; put the exponents into a consistent notation; check moments and independence; then decide whether a CLT applies and how to normalize. These five steps expose the most common errors: an exponent off by one, a nonexistent moment, or a missing scale factor.

Scale-Free Networks and Preferential Attachment: Deriving the Distribution from the Mechanism

We use nnn for the number of nodes, MMM for the total number of edges, and mmm for the number of edges introduced by each new node in the BA model.

What Does a Network Represent, and What Does Scale-Free Mean?

A network represents a system through nodes (vertices) and edges (links). Whether the model is appropriate depends first on how these are defined. The Internet can be represented by computers or routers linked by communication connections; the WWW by web pages linked by directed hyperlinks; and a citation network by papers linked by directed citations. Other examples are power stations/substations and transmission lines in a power grid, people and friendships in a friendship network, metabolites and reactions in a metabolic network, neurons and synapses in a neural network, and species and predation relations in a food web. Direction, weight, and the level of detail used to define nodes depend on the question.

Degree and the Degree Distribution

In a simple undirected graph, the degree kik_iki​ of node iii is its number of neighbors. If a node is selected uniformly at random, the probability that its degree is kkk is

p(k)=nkn,∑kp(k)=1,⟨k⟩=∑kkp(k)=2Mn,p(k)=\frac{n_k}{n},\qquad \sum_k p(k)=1,\qquad \langle k\rangle=\sum_k k p(k)=\frac{2M}{n}, p(k)=nnk​​,k∑​p(k)=1,⟨k⟩=k∑​kp(k)=n2M​,

Here nkn_knk​ is the number of nodes whose degree is exactly kkk. For a directed graph, in-degree and out-degree distributions must be considered separately. The defining feature of a scale-free network is an approximately power-law tail in its degree distribution; a visually tangled drawing is not sufficient:

p(k)∼Ck−γ,S(k)=Pr⁡(K≥k)∼C′k−(γ−1),α=γ−1.p(k)\sim Ck^{-\gamma},\qquad S(k)=\Pr(K\geq k)\sim C'k^{-(\gamma-1)},\qquad \alpha=\gamma-1. p(k)∼Ck−γ,S(k)=Pr(K≥k)∼C′k−(γ−1),α=γ−1.

For discrete degrees, p(k)p(k)p(k) is a probability mass function; it is a probability density only in the continuous approximation. S(k)S(k)S(k) is the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF), whereas the ordinary CDF is F(k)=Pr⁡(K≤k)F(k)=\Pr(K\leq k)F(k)=Pr(K≤k). Do not label a decreasing power-law tail as the ordinary CDF.

What the Exponent Means

A power-law tail makes high-degree nodes more common than an exponential or Poisson tail does. Such high-degree nodes are called hubs. Power-law scale-free behavior does not generally require γ<3\gamma<3γ<3; the range 1<γ<31<\gamma<31<γ<3 is important because the second moment diverges in an ideal distribution with no upper cutoff. The condition is ⟨Kr⟩<∞\langle K^r\rangle<\infty⟨Kr⟩<∞ if and only if γ>r+1\gamma>r+1γ>r+1; at equality, the divergence is typically logarithmic. Thus, for 2<γ<32<\gamma<32<γ<3, the mean is finite while the variance is infinite; γ=3\gamma=3γ=3 is the boundary for the second moment. Real finite networks have a maximum degree, and their finite-sample moments are finite.

Example: interpreting exponents. A degree distribution with γ≈3.4\gamma\approx3.4γ≈3.4 has a finite second moment under an ideal pure power-law model. A distribution with γ≈3\gamma\approx3γ≈3 lies at the boundary. An exponent above three does not rule out a power law, and a power-law fit to one network does not establish that all real networks are strictly scale-free.

Counting Nodes and Edges

For a graph with 8 nodes and 10 edges, including one isolated node, the degrees must sum to 20=2×1020=2\times1020=2×10. This provides a consistency check on an edge count. In a drawing, a crossing without a node marker does not create a node, and arrows used only as labels are not edges.

The BA Model: Growth and Preferential Attachment

Start with a seed network containing n0n_0n0​ nodes and M0M_0M0​ edges. At each step, add one node and connect it to mmm existing nodes:

n(t)=n0+t,M(t)=M0+mt,Πi=ki∑jkj,∑iΠi=1.n(t)=n_0+t,\quad M(t)=M_0+mt,\quad \Pi_i=\frac{k_i}{\sum_j k_j},\quad \sum_i\Pi_i=1. n(t)=n0​+t,M(t)=M0​+mt,Πi​=∑j​kj​ki​​,i∑​Πi​=1.

Growth continually introduces new nodes. Preferential attachment makes existing nodes with higher degree more likely to receive new edges. The seed must give a nonzero denominator and contain enough existing nodes; normally m≤n0m\leq n_0m≤n0​ is required. Distinguishing the initial edge count M0M_0M0​ from the initial node count n0n_0n0​ avoids ambiguity.

The continuous approximation reveals the exponent conveniently; the master equation also gives the prefactor of the discrete degree probabilities. In the large-time approximation, that node increases its degree by one in the next step with probability k/(2t)k/(2t)k/(2t), giving

q(k,ti,t+1)=k−12tq(k−1,ti,t)+(1−k2t)q(k,ti,t).q(k,t_i,t+1)=\frac{k-1}{2t}q(k-1,t_i,t) +\left(1-\frac{k}{2t}\right)q(k,t_i,t). q(k,ti​,t+1)=2tk−1​q(k−1,ti​,t)+(1−2tk​)q(k,ti​,t).

The first term is inflow from degree k−1k-1k−1 after receiving an edge; the second retains nodes that already had degree kkk and receive no edge. Choosing mmm different targets without replacement in a finite network must not be described as an exact collection of independent Bernoulli trials.

Testing the Mechanism and Comparing with Erdős–Rényi Networks

Why Are Both Mechanisms Needed?

Removing preferential attachment while retaining growth produces a rapidly decaying degree distribution. Removing growth and keeping a fixed node set also fails to maintain the BA model's growing power-law state. This explains how the two ingredients work together in the BA model; it does not establish that every power law must come from BA. A static graph can also be constructed directly with a specified power-law degree distribution.

A useful calculation is to choose the targets of new edges uniformly among existing nodes. Then dki/dt≃m/t\mathrm dk_i/\mathrm dt\simeq m/tdki​/dt≃m/t, giving ki(t)≃m+mln⁡(t/ti)k_i(t)\simeq m+m\ln(t/t_i)ki​(t)≃m+mln(t/ti​). Combining this with uniformly distributed birth times gives the approximate tail probability Pr⁡(K≥k)≃exp⁡[−(k−m)/m]\Pr(K\geq k)\simeq\exp[-(k-m)/m]Pr(K≥k)≃exp[−(k−m)/m], demonstrating that growth alone does not automatically produce a power law. Preferential attachment can be investigated empirically by measuring whether the probability of receiving new links increases with existing degree, for example in citation or collaboration networks.

Definition of the ER Model

In G(n,p)G(n,p)G(n,p), fix nnn nodes and connect each pair of distinct nodes independently by an undirected edge with probability ppp. There are no self-loops or parallel edges. Since there are (n2)\binom n2(2n​) possible edges,

M∼Bin⁡ ⁣((n2),p),E[M]=pn(n−1)2.M\sim\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(\binom n2,p\right),\qquad \mathrm E[M]=p\frac{n(n-1)}2. M∼Bin((2n​),p),E[M]=p2n(n−1)​.

The quantity pn(n−1)/2pn(n-1)/2pn(n−1)/2 is the expected number of edges; the realized edge count is random. A single node has n−1n-1n−1 potential neighbors, so

K∼Bin⁡(n−1,p),Pr⁡(K=k)=(n−1k)pk(1−p)n−1−k,K\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n-1,p),\qquad \Pr(K=k)=\binom{n-1}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-1-k}, K∼Bin(n−1,p),Pr(K=k)=(kn−1​)pk(1−p)n−1−k,

c=E[K]=(n−1)p,Var⁡(K)=(n−1)p(1−p).c=\mathrm E[K]=(n-1)p,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=(n-1)p(1-p). c=E[K]=(n−1)p,Var(K)=(n−1)p(1−p).

Here ccc is the theoretical mean-degree parameter; the realized mean degree of a particular graph is still 2M/n2M/n2M/n.

The Poisson Limit for a Large Sparse Network

Let n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, taking p=c/(n−1)→0p=c/(n-1)\to0p=c/(n−1)→0 while holding ccc fixed. For a fixed kkk,

(n−1k)≃(n−1)kk!,(1−cn−1)n−1−k⟶e−c.\binom{n-1}{k}\simeq\frac{(n-1)^k}{k!},\qquad \left(1-\frac{c}{n-1}\right)^{n-1-k}\longrightarrow e^{-c}. (kn−1​)≃k!(n−1)k​,(1−n−1c​)n−1−k⟶e−c.

Substitution into the binomial probability gives

Pr⁡(K=k)⟶e−cckk!,E[K]=Var⁡(K)=c(Poisson limit).\boxed{\Pr(K=k)\longrightarrow e^{-c}\frac{c^k}{k!}},\qquad \mathrm E[K]=\operatorname{Var}(K)=c\quad\text{(Poisson limit)}. Pr(K=k)⟶e−ck!ck​​,E[K]=Var(K)=c(Poisson limit).

In particular, the probability of an isolated node is p(0)=e−cp(0)=e^{-c}p(0)=e−c, so the expected number of isolated nodes is approximately ne−cne^{-c}ne−c. This rare-event limit is not the central limit theorem. If ccc is also large, a Poisson distribution can be further approximated by N(c,c)\mathcal N(c,c)N(c,c). More generally, a binomial distribution admits a normal approximation when both (n−1)p(n-1)p(n−1)p and (n−1)(1−p)(n-1)(1-p)(n−1)(1−p) are sufficiently large. The sparse limit with fixed ccc does not by itself make the degree distribution normal.

The Main Differences Between ER and BA

ER fixes the node set and assigns independent, identically distributed edge indicators. Degrees concentrate around ccc and their tail decays rapidly. BA continually adds nodes, makes attachment depend on existing degree, has ⟨k⟩→2m\langle k\rangle\to2m⟨k⟩→2m, and produces p(k)∼k−3p(k)\sim k^{-3}p(k)∼k−3 with more prominent high-degree nodes. ER graphs can still contain nodes whose degree exceeds the mean. Relative degree homogeneity does not mean that the maximum degree equals the mean.

Typical Scale-Free Network Problems: Calculations, Derivations, and Checks

Example 1: Growth of an Individual Node

In a BA model with m=2m=2m=2, a node enters at ti=25t_i=25ti​=25. Find its expected degree at T=400T=400T=400.

ki(400)≃2400/25=8.k_i(400)\simeq2\sqrt{400/25}=8. ki​(400)≃2400/25​=8.

To estimate the time needed to reach degree 202020, solve 20=2T/2520=2\sqrt{T/25}20=2T/25​, which gives T=2500T=2500T=2500. This is a mean-field time scale; the time at which an individual random node actually reaches that degree fluctuates.

p(2)=12,p(3)=25p(2)=15,p(4)=36p(3)=110.p(2)=\frac12,\qquad p(3)=\frac25p(2)=\frac15, \qquad p(4)=\frac36p(3)=\frac1{10}. p(2)=21​,p(3)=52​p(2)=51​,p(4)=63​p(3)=101​.

Pr⁡(K≥10)=2⋅310⋅11=355≃0.0545.\Pr(K\geq10)=\frac{2\cdot3}{10\cdot11}=\frac3{55}\simeq0.0545. Pr(K≥10)=10⋅112⋅3​=553​≃0.0545.

The expected count is therefore about 545545545. The continuous approximation gives m2/102=0.04m^2/10^2=0.04m2/102=0.04; it captures the scaling law and need not match the discrete result at a relatively small integer threshold.

Example 3: ER Network Parameters

Take n=1000,p=0.004n=1000,p=0.004n=1000,p=0.004:

c=999×0.004=3.996,E[M]=1000×3.9962=1998.c=999\times0.004=3.996,\qquad \mathrm E[M]=\frac{1000\times3.996}{2}=1998. c=999×0.004=3.996,E[M]=21000×3.996​=1998.

Pr⁡(K=0)≃e−3.996≃0.0184,E[nisolated]≃18.4.\Pr(K=0)\simeq e^{-3.996}\simeq0.0184, \qquad \mathrm E[n_{\rm isolated}]\simeq18.4. Pr(K=0)≃e−3.996≃0.0184,E[nisolated​]≃18.4.

Example 4: Reading an Exponent from a Plot

If the degree probability p(k)p(k)p(k) has slope −2.7-2.7−2.7 on a log–log plot, then γ=2.7\gamma=2.7γ=2.7, and the CCDF should have slope approximately −1.7-1.7−1.7. If a CCDF instead has slope −2-2−2, then γ=3\gamma=3γ=3, consistent with the standard BA exponent. This exponent alone does not prove that the generating mechanism is BA.

The Shortest Complete Derivation Answer

A complete continuous derivation should include Πi=ki/∑jkj\Pi_i=k_i/\sum_j k_jΠi​=ki​/∑j​kj​, ∑jkj≃2mt\sum_jk_j\simeq2mt∑j​kj​≃2mt, k˙i=ki/(2t)\dot k_i=k_i/(2t)k˙i​=ki​/(2t), ki(ti)=mk_i(t_i)=mki​(ti​)=m, ki(t)=m(t/ti)1/2k_i(t)=m(t/t_i)^{1/2}ki​(t)=m(t/ti​)1/2, uniformly distributed birth times, F(k)=1−m2/k2F(k)=1-m^2/k^2F(k)=1−m2/k2, and p(k)=2m2k−3p(k)=2m^2k^{-3}p(k)=2m2k−3. A complete master-equation derivation should include inflow, outflow, the δkm\delta_{km}δkm​ birth term, stationary fractions represented by Nk(t)≃tp(k)N_k(t)\simeq t p(k)Nk​(t)≃tp(k), the boundary value p(m)p(m)p(m), the recurrence, and cancellation of its product.

Common Mistakes

  • Πi\Pi_iΠi​ describes the attachment tendency of one new edge; mΠim\Pi_imΠi​ gives the approximate expected degree increase per time step.

  • A "stationary degree distribution" means the fractions stop changing. It does not mean that the node count or individual degrees stop growing.

  • γ\gammaγ is the degree-probability exponent, whereas α=γ−1\alpha=\gamma-1α=γ−1 is the tail-probability exponent. For BA, γ=3,α=2\gamma=3,\alpha=2γ=3,α=2.

  • Distinguish the continuous approximation 2m2/k32m^2/k^32m2/k3 from the discrete result 2m(m+1)/[k(k+1)(k+2)]2m(m+1)/[k(k+1)(k+2)]2m(m+1)/[k(k+1)(k+2)] and state which one you are using.

  • G(n,p)G(n,p)G(n,p) fixes an edge probability. The ER model G(n,M)G(n,M)G(n,M) fixes the edge count instead, so its edge indicators must not be assumed independent.

Network Basics: Representations, Graph Types, Connectivity, and Matrix Calculations

Unless stated otherwise, graphs are finite and have no self-loops or parallel edges. Directed and weighted cases are identified explicitly.

Basic Terminology and Two Graph Representations

Write a graph as G=(V,E)G=(V,E)G=(V,E), with node set VVV and edge set EEE. An undirected edge {i,j}\{i,j\}{i,j} represents a symmetric relation; a directed edge (i,j)(i,j)(i,j) represents i→ji\to ji→j. A simple graph has no self-loops or parallel edges; "simple" does not mean that its structure is regular. Complex networks often model systems with heterogeneous degrees and intricate connectivity. The word "complex" is not itself a unique graph-theoretic test.

Adjacency Matrices and Adjacency Lists

First specify the node ordering, then define the adjacency matrix. Rows are sources and columns are targets:

Aij={1,i→j exists (undirected: i adjacent to j),0,otherwise.A_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,&i\to j\text{ exists (undirected: }i\text{ adjacent to }j\text{)},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} Aij​={1,0,​i→j exists (undirected: i adjacent to j),otherwise.​

For an undirected graph, the first case means that the two nodes are adjacent. An adjacency list records each node's neighbors. For directed graphs it usually lists out-neighbors; in-neighbors can be stored separately when needed. A simple undirected graph satisfies A=ATA=A^{\mathsf T}A=AT and Aii=0A_{ii}=0Aii​=0. Each edge appears twice in the matrix and once in the adjacency list of each endpoint.

Consider a four-node graph with edge set {12,13,23,34}\{12,13,23,34\}{12,13,23,34}. Ordering the nodes as 1,2,3,41,2,3,41,2,3,4 gives

A=[0110101011010010],(k1,k2,k3,k4)=(2,2,3,1).A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&1&0\\1&0&1&0\\1&1&0&1\\0&0&1&0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad(k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4)=(2,2,3,1). A=⎣⎢⎢⎢⎡​0110​1010​1101​0010​⎦⎥⎥⎥⎤​,(k1​,k2​,k3​,k4​)=(2,2,3,1).

The adjacency lists are 1:{2,3}1:\{2,3\}1:{2,3}, 2:{1,3}2:\{1,3\}2:{1,3}, 3:{1,2,4}3:\{1,2,4\}3:{1,2,4}, and 4:{3}4:\{3\}4:{3}. Row sums give the degrees; their total is 888, so M=4M=4M=4.

Walks, Paths, Cycles, and Subgraphs

  • A walk is a sequence of adjacent nodes and may repeat nodes or edges. Its length is the number of traversed edges.

  • A path conventionally has no repeated nodes. If a question uses a broader informal definition, state the convention you adopt. Each consecutive pair must be joined by an edge, and directions must also match in a directed graph.

  • A cycle returns to its starting node without repeating any other node. In a simple undirected graph, a cycle contains at least 333 edges.

  • A subgraph selects some nodes and some of the original edges between them. An induced subgraph selects nodes and retains every original edge between the selected nodes.

Two nodes are connected if there is a path between them. A connected graph has a path between every pair of nodes. A connected component is a maximal connected subgraph: no additional node can be included while preserving connectivity. An isolated node is itself a component. The largest connected component has the greatest number of nodes; "maximal" and "largest" are different concepts.

Multiple Components and Block Matrices

Group nodes from the same component together. Reordering both rows and columns gives

A′=PAPT=[A10⋯0A2⋯⋮⋮⋱].A'=PAP^{\mathsf T}=\begin{bmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots\\0&A_2&\cdots\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots\end{bmatrix}. A′=PAPT=⎣⎢⎢⎡​A1​0⋮​0A2​⋮​⋯⋯⋱​⎦⎥⎥⎤​.

PPP represents only a node permutation. There are no edges between components, so the off-diagonal blocks are zero. This applies to undirected components and to distinct weak components of a directed graph. Different strong components can have one-way edges between them, so ordering nodes by strong components need not make the adjacency matrix block diagonal.
